title: Episode 90: The Centralia Mine Fire: The Town That Burned from Below
description:
In May 1962, a routine landfill cleanup in the anthracite coal town of Centralia, Pennsylvania ignited an exposed subterranean coal seam. Over six decades later, an inferno still rages hundreds of feet beneath abandoned streets, poisonous sulfur vents, and cracked highways.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we journey into the anthracite coal country of eastern Pennsylvania, where a bustling twentieth-century mining borough vanished not from flood, war, or storm, but from a subterranean demon born of a single match. In May nineteen sixty-two, volunteer firefighters set out to clean up a municipal dump. What they inadvertently ignited was the sprawling, interconnected labyrinth of the Buck Mountain coal seam. Sixty years later, that subterranean fire is still burning at over one thousand degrees Fahrenheit, transforming a community of over a thousand residents into a smoking, toxic ghost town whose zip code was revoked by the federal government. Here is George with the full, harrowing chronicle of Centralia.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: ANTHRACITE AND THE BOROUGH OF CENTRALIA
In the rugged ridge-and-valley country of Columbia County, Pennsylvania, the borough of Centralia was built upon the greatest deposit of anthracite coal in the Western Hemisphere. Unlike the soft bituminous coal found in western Pennsylvania and West Virginia, anthracite was hard, lustrous, and nearly pure carbon. It burned with an intense, smokeless blue flame, heating the parlor stoves and powering the locomotives of America's industrial revolution throughout the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Centralia was chartered in eighteen sixty-six, quickly growing into a vibrant, tight-knit enclave of immigrant families—primarily Irish, Ukrainian, Polish, and Italian—who carved a civilization out of the rugged Appalachian hillside.
Beneath their homes, churches, and paved avenues lay miles of honeycomb mine tunnels, vertical shafts, and forgotten gangways where generations of men and boys had wielded pickaxes and black powder. The borough bustled with five churches, multiple fraternal lodges, grocery stores, and neighborhoods filled with pride. Yet life above the coal had always been intimately intertwined with danger. Cave-ins, black damp gas, and surface subsidences were common hazards accepted by mining families as the unavoidable price of anthracite extraction. The townsfolk knew the coal under their feet was vast and combustible, but none could have imagined that the town's ultimate destruction would come not from a sudden shaft collapse, but from a careless spark ignited in broad daylight.
By the early nineteen sixties, many of the deep commercial collieries had shuttered due to rising competition from heating oil and natural gas, leaving behind an unregulated subterranean labyrinth of abandoned timber-braced tunnels. Centralia's municipal leaders struggled with local waste disposal, eventually choosing an abandoned sixty-foot strip-mine pit just south of Odd Fellows Cemetery as the town's primary landfill. The pit opened directly into exposed, unsealed veins of Buck Mountain anthracite, a geological fuse waiting for a match.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE MEMORIAL DAY CLEANUP
In May nineteen sixty-two, with Memorial Day weekend approaching, the Centralia Borough Council met to discuss the unsightly condition of the new municipal dump. Heaps of household trash, paper, and debris spilled along the edge of the pit, creating a foul odor within sight of the nearby cemetery where families would soon gather to honor fallen veterans. The council resolved to hire local volunteer firefighters to clean the site by doing what small towns across rural America routinely did: setting the accumulated garbage ablaze under controlled supervision and then dousing the embers with fire hoses.
On Sunday, May twenty-seventh, five volunteer firefighters arrived at the strip pit and ignited the refuse. By evening, the surface flames had consumed the trash, and the men saturated the smoking embers with thousands of gallons of water until no surface flames remained. The firefighters departed, believing the routine job was finished. But deep inside the refuse pit, concealed beneath layers of shale and discarded household garbage, a hidden aperture led directly into an unsealed coal outcrop. Unbeknownst to anyone on the surface, glowing embers had fallen through the rubble, finding a continuous supply of oxygen and igniting the raw face of the coal seam.
Two days later, on May twenty-ninth, smoke was spotted rising once again from the pit floor. Firefighters returned with booster hoses and soaked the smoldering mound a second time. Yet on June fourth, June ninth, and repeatedly throughout early summer, fresh plumes of foul-smelling smoke billowed from subterranean crevices. When a bulldozer was finally brought in to dig out the smoldering garbage, operators recoiled in shock: beneath the trash, the pit floor was cherry-red, and thick clouds of carbon monoxide hissed from deep cracks in the bedrock. The fire was no longer burning surface trash; it had migrated deep into the abandoned mines.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE POISON IN THE BASEMENTS
Throughout the remainder of the nineteen sixties and into the nineteen seventies, state and federal mining agencies made sporadic, poorly funded attempts to contain the advancing underground blaze. Excavation trenches were dug, fly-ash slurry was pumped into boreholes to seal off oxygen, and clay barriers were constructed in surrounding pits. But every engineering effort was delayed by jurisdictional squabbles, bureaucratic inertia, and a fundamental failure to grasp the sheer scope of the subterranean inferno. The fire leaped across planned barrier trenches through unmapped bootleg tunnels, fueled by millions of tons of high-grade anthracite that generated temperatures exceeding twelve hundred degrees Fahrenheit.
For the residents living above, daily life slowly morphed into a surreal and terrifying nightmare. Basements began to warm to unnatural temperatures, radiating heat through concrete foundations. Garden vegetables in backyard plots cooked in the soil before they could be harvested, and steam poured from sidewalk gutters in the dead of winter. Far more sinister was the invisible enemy: toxic gases produced by the subterranean combustion. Carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, and methane seeped upward through cellar walls, floor drains, and water pipes, silently accumulating in living rooms while families slept.
The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources began installing continuous carbon monoxide monitors in Centralia homes, equipping bedrooms with shrieking battery-powered alarms. Residents slept with windows open in freezing blizzards, fearful of suffocating in their beds. Houseplants withered within hours, and pet canaries and dogs died mysteriously. In nineteen seventy-nine, local gas station owner and former mayor John Coddington lowered a measuring stick into his underground gasoline storage tanks to check inventory, only to pull it out hot to the touch. When he lowered a thermometer, he discovered his fuel supply was sitting at an astonishing one hundred and seventy-two degrees Fahrenheit, creating an imminent risk of a catastrophic vapor explosion directly beneath Route sixty-one.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CHASM IN TODD DOMBOSKI'S BACKYARD
Despite rising carbon monoxide alarms and blazing borehole temperatures, the crisis in Centralia remained largely ignored by the wider American public until Valentine's Day in nineteen eighty-one. On that crisp Saturday morning, twelve-year-old Todd Domboski was walking across his grandmother's backyard on Locust Avenue. He noticed a small wisp of sulfurous steam rising from beneath the roots of a modest fruit tree and stepped toward it out of curiosity. Without warning, the earth beneath his boots liquefied into a bottomless chasm.
The ground collapsed into a four-foot-wide, one-hundred-and-fifty-foot-deep sinkhole caused by the underground fire consuming the supporting coal pillars below. As young Todd plummeted down the smoking throat of the pit, he instinctively reached outward, grasping a tree root with his bare fingers as sulfurous gas and superheated steam engulfed his body. His desperate screams pierced the morning quiet, alerting his fourteen-year-old cousin, Eric Wolfgang, who dashed across the lawn, threw himself onto his stomach at the crumbling edge of the pit, and grabbed Todd's wrists just as the root gave way, hauling him out of the abyss seconds before the pit swallowed him whole.
When emergency responders arrived and lowered measuring instruments into the steaming hole, they recorded lethal concentrations of carbon monoxide and air temperatures exceeding three hundred and fifty degrees Fahrenheit. Had Todd fallen all the way, death from toxic asphyxiation and thermal burns would have occurred within minutes. The terrifying image of a child nearly swallowed alive by an underground fire in his own backyard was broadcast on evening news programs across the globe, shattering the government's narrative that the town remained safe for human habitation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE TOWN THAT DIVIDED ITSELF
The near-tragedy of Todd Domboski galvanized national media attention and transformed Centralia into a powder keg of political and emotional conflict. In nineteen eighty-three, the United States Bureau of Mines released a comprehensive engineering study outlining potential solutions. The report concluded that fully extinguishing the mine fire would require a massive strip-mining operation to dig out the entire mountain down to four hundred feet, at an estimated cost exceeding six hundred and sixty million dollars—equivalent to more than two billion dollars today—with absolutely no guarantee of success.
Instead, Congress appropriated forty-two million dollars in nineteen eighty-four to execute a voluntary buyout program, offering to purchase homes at fair market value and relocate residents to neighboring towns like Mount Carmel and Ashland. But the buyout tore Centralia's social fabric in two. A passionate faction of residents, convinced that the town was a death trap and determined to protect their children from toxic poisoning, demanded immediate evacuation and demolition. Another deeply rooted faction of lifelong coal families, suspecting a grand conspiracy by energy conglomerates to drive them off valuable coal reserves, refused to surrender the land their immigrant ancestors had settled.
Heated arguments erupted at church gatherings, neighbors ceased speaking across fence lines, and graffiti appeared on storefronts labeling buyout participants as cowards and traitors. Over one thousand residents took the federal buyout and moved away, watching in heartbreak as government bulldozers arrived to demolish their childhood homes, leaving behind vast, empty grassy lots crisscrossed by abandoned paved streets and disconnected concrete front steps.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE REVOCATION OF A ZIP CODE
By nineteen ninety-two, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania moved decisively to close the chapter on Centralia by invoking eminent domain over all remaining private property within the borough limits. Officials declared that the continuing expansion of the fire, which now encompassed more than four hundred acres and was steadily marching toward neighboring Byrnesville, rendered the area permanently uninhabitable. State police and highway officials closed Pennsylvania Route sixty-one, which had buckled and split apart under the intense subterranean heat, carving three-foot fissures that emitted sulfurous smoke directly through the asphalt.
Traffic was permanently rerouted along a bypass, leaving the abandoned section of Route sixty-one to become the infamous 'Graffiti Highway,' a bizarre post-apocalyptic stretch of roadway where artists and tourists from around the world gathered to spray-paint vibrant murals across smoking fractures. In two thousand and two, the United States Postal Service took the rare step of formally revoking Centralia's zip code—one-seven-nine-two-seven—erasing the community from the official postal map of the nation.
Yet a small, stubborn band of holdouts refused to leave. Fewer than a dozen elderly residents fought the state in court for over two decades, defending their right to remain in the homes where they had lived their entire lives. In twenty-thirteen, a historic legal settlement was finally reached: the state allowed the remaining seven residents to live out their natural lives in their homes under a life tenancy agreement, with the stipulation that upon their passing, ownership of the properties would revert permanently to the commonwealth for demolition.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEGACY OF THE BURNING MOUNTAIN
Today, Centralia stands as a haunting, modern-day Pompeii, an eerie testament to the devastating unintended consequences of human environmental neglect. The borough's paved streets still form neat rectangular grids across the hillside, but they lead to empty forest clearings where living rooms, kitchens, and schoolyards once stood. Street signs stand sentinel over vacant fields, while telephone poles carry dead wires through overgrown stands of birch and sumac. High on the hill overlooking the ruins stands the Ukrainian Catholic Church of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, its onion dome gleaming against the sky, still holding weekly divine liturgy on solid rock above the burning coal.
Deep underground, the Buck Mountain seam continues to burn unhindered. Mining geologists estimate that the subterranean fire currently occupies over four hundred acres, fueled by vast reserves of anthracite that contain enough combustible energy to burn for another one to two centuries. On cold winter mornings, white plumes of sulfuric vapor still rise through vents in the hillside, curling upward through snow-dusted trees like the breath of a slumbering dragon.
Centralia serves as an enduring cautionary tale of industrial hubris, environmental fragility, and governmental procrastination. It proved that the ground beneath our feet, which we assume to be eternal and unyielding, can be irrevocably compromised by a single moment of carelessness. What was once a thriving borough of immigrant dreamers and proud coal miners now belongs to the fire, an eternal subterranean flame that has outlived the town it consumed.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Centralia remains an eternal flame beneath the Pennsylvania mountains, a somber warning of industrial neglect and the enduring power of nature. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we travel to the Allegheny Mountains for the terrifying story of the Great Johnstown Flood of eighteen eighty-nine.
